title: The great exhibition
articleHtml:
A 

Philosopher Karl Marx and naturalist Charles Darwin may once have rubbed shoulders as they gazed upon the world's largest diamond. Just metres away, authors Charlotte Bronte and George Eliot may have passed one another as they used the world's first pay toilets. Where could these encounters have taken place? Only at the Great Exhibition of the Works of Industry of All Nations (usually just called the Great Exhibition), one of the most impressive spectacles ever staged. It was held in London's Hyde Park between May and October 1851, and everyone from renowned scientists to humble shopkeepers walked excitedly through its doors.

 

B 

The Great Exhibition was designed to showcase treasures and inventions from around the globe, but more importantly to demonstrate that Britain was the world leader in industry. This was essential propaganda at the height of the British empire, and Prince Albert - husband of Queen Victoria - was instrumental in organising the event. He proved a remarkably successful coordinator. Over six million people, a third of Britain's population at the time, came to view the 100,000 objects on display, generating the equivalent of £20 million or more in today's money. With this revenue, Albert paid for the Great Exhibition's legacy: the Victoria and Albert Museum, Natural History Museum and Science Museum, which remain among London's most popular attractions today. He also established a scholarship fund for industrial research that continues to make awards in the twenty-first century.

 

C 

Initially, it had been predicted that the Exhibition would make a loss. Though season tickets cost as much as three guineas (more than £300 today), day passes were the most popular and sold for just one shilling (roughly five pounds today). People snapped up these bargain tickets in huge numbers. Factory owners all over Britain sent their employees to learn from the show, while local vicars organised trips for their parishioners and for schoolchildren. Rail companies offered discounted tickets so that access was not denied to those in far-off counties. Such was the pull of the Exhibition,it was reported that one woman walked over 300 miles from Cornwall, on the south-west coast of England, just to see it.

 

D 

The principal draw of the Great Exhibition is generally assumed to have been its novelty. It is often described as the first world 'expo' (from the French word exposition, meaning exhibition), and it is true that the public had rarely experienced anything quite like it. But it is not entirely accurate to say that the Great Exhibition was the first of its type, as France had been organising its own industrial expos since 1798.These took place largely under the international radar until 1844, when the tenth French expo prompted a number of imitations from Madrid to St Petersburg. However, it hosted under 4,000 exhibitors compared to the Great Exhibition's 15,000. So ultimately, it may not have been the novelty of the latter that inspired such awe, but the scale and quality of the exhibits.

 

E 

As well as the Koh-i-Noor (then the world's largest diamond)and Daria-i-Noor (an exceptionally rare pink diamond) from India, visitors to the Great Exhibition saw inventions that now seem commonplace but were ground-breaking in Victorian times. There were printing presses and adding machines, surgical instruments and velocipedes (precursors to the modern bicycle). France brought exquisite silks and tapestries; Canada exhibited a fire engine and a range of luxurious furs; Russia showed porcelain vases that stood twice the height of the average visitor. There was even a folding piano, designed so that sailors could entertain themselves at sea, although this particular innovation was never to find a place in the mass market!

 

F 

Arguably, the greatest 'invention' on display at the Great Exhibition was the building that housed it. Designed by Joseph Paxton specifically for the event, it resembled a giant greenhouse and became affectionately known as the Crystal Palace. At more than half a kilometre long, and using modern materials such as sheet glass and cast iron, the building was not only striking but demonstrated Britain's engineering prowess. After the Exhibition it was moved from Hyde Park to Sydenham, south London, where it breathed new life into a previously sleepy suburb. New train stations and pleasure gardens were constructed in the vicinity of the building, which in its new home was chiefly used as a convention centre but also served as a naval training base during World War I. Sadly, the Palace was destroyed by accidental fire in 1936, but its name lives on in the park which used to surround it - and in the Premier League football team, Crystal Palace.

 

G 

Today the Great Exhibition is remembered as one of Victorian Britain's greatest achievements, a manifestation of the country's industrial might. But it is also of immense importance for students and collectors of nineteenth century design, since works of so many types, and from so many nations, were gathered together there. The Exhibition's catalogue, which runs to over 700 pages and contains sumptuous illustrations characteristic of the era, has now been digitised for public access; meanwhile original souvenirs, such as tickets and programmes, change hands for hundreds of proud. Thanks to contemporary technology an event like the Exhibition is never likely to be repeated, so perhaps it is no surprise that it has assumed such legendary status.
